lessons.title: Saying hello
lessons.goal: Greet people at any time of day and ask how they are.

dialogue.en: Good morning, Lucas. How are you?

tip.title: Good morning, good afternoon, good night
tip.text: Buenos días is used until about noon, buenas tardes until it gets dark, and buenas noches after dark. Día is a boy word even though it ends in a, so it is buenos días; tardes and noches are girl words, so they take buenas. Buenas noches is both hello in the evening and good night at bedtime.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask a friend "How are you?"

lessons.title: Polite hellos and goodbyes
lessons.goal: Greet an adult politely and say goodbye in different ways.

dialogue.es: Buenas tardes, señora Díaz. ¿Cómo está usted?
dialogue.en: Good afternoon, Mrs. Díaz. How are you?
Bye, Mrs. Díaz! See you tomorrow!

tip.title: Tú and usted
tip.text: Spanish has two ways to say you. Use tú with family, friends and kids, and usted with adults you don't know well, teachers and older people. The verb changes too: ¿Cómo estás? is for a friend, ¿Cómo está usted? is for a grown-up like Mrs. Díaz. When in doubt with an adult, usted is the safe choice.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "See you tomorrow"?

exercises.en: Ask your teacher: How are you?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Good night" at bedtime?

lessons.title: Please and thank you
lessons.goal: Say please, thank you, sorry and excuse me.

dialogue.en: Yes, please. Thank you very much!
Excuse me, Mrs. Díaz. See you later!

tip.title: Perdón, lo siento, con permiso
tip.text: Perdón is for small slips, like bumping into someone, or to get someone's attention. Lo siento means I'm sorry, for when something sad or bigger happens. Con permiso asks to get by, or to leave the table or the room. When someone says gracias, answer de nada.

exercises.prompt: You need to walk past someone. What do you say?

lessons.title: What's your name?
lessons.goal: Ask someone's name, say yours and say nice to meet you.

dialogue.en: Hi! I'm Sofía. What's your name?

dialogue.es: Buenas tardes. Mi nombre es Miguel. ¿Cómo se llama usted?
dialogue.en: Good afternoon. My name is Miguel. What's your name?
My name is Carmen. Nice to meet you.

tip.title: Me llamo and encantado
tip.text: Me llamo Ana means my name is Ana; word for word it is I call myself Ana. Mucho gusto works for everyone. Encantado changes: a boy or man says encantado, a girl or woman says encantada. Answer either one with igualmente, likewise.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask a friend "What's your name?"

exercises.en: Ask an adult politely: What's your name?

lessons.title: Where are you from?
lessons.goal: Say where you are from and where you live, and introduce people.

dialogue.es: Soy de Arizona. Vivo en Sahuarita. ¿Y tú?
dialogue.en: I'm from Arizona. I live in Sahuarita. And you?

dialogue.es: Igualmente. Daniel, te presento a mi mamá.
dialogue.en: Likewise. Daniel, this is my mom.

dialogue.es: Mamá, ella es mi amiga Ana.
dialogue.en: Mom, this is my friend Ana.

tip.title: Él, ella, amigo, amiga
tip.text: Él with an accent means he; el without one means the. A friend who is a boy is mi amigo, a friend who is a girl is mi amiga. Use soy de for where you are from and vivo en for where you live. Te presento a introduces someone to a friend; with an adult, people say le presento a.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I live in Sahuarita"?

lessons.title: A little Spanish
lessons.goal: Say how much Spanish you speak and ask people to slow down or repeat.

dialogue.en: Hi! What's your name? Where are you from?

dialogue.es: Perdón, no entiendo. Más despacio, por favor.
dialogue.en: Sorry, I don't understand. Slower, please.

dialogue.es: ¡Ah! Me llamo Mateo. Hablo un poco de español. ¿Hablas inglés?
dialogue.en: Oh! My name is Mateo. I speak a little Spanish. Do you speak English?
Ma'am, how do you say "ball" in Spanish?

tip.title: Saying no
tip.text: To make a sentence negative, put no right before the verb: hablo is I speak, no hablo is I don't speak. No entiendo works the same way. Spanish usually leaves out yo (I), because the -o at the end of hablo already tells you who is speaking. ¿Puede repetir? is polite for adults; to a friend, say ¿puedes repetir?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I don't understand"?

exercises.answer: How do you say it in Spanish?

exercises.en: Say: Can you repeat that, please?

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Where are you from?"

lessons.title: Zero to ten
lessons.goal: Count from 0 to 10.

dialogue.en: Mateo, how do you say "ten" in Spanish?

dialogue.es: ¡Diez! Uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez.
dialogue.en: Ten! One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

dialogue.es: Mateo: diez, nueve, ocho, siete, seis, cinco, cuatro, tres, dos, uno...
dialogue.en: Mateo: ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one...

tip.title: Say them clearly
tip.text: In Mexican Spanish, c before e or i sounds like s: cero is SEH-roh and cinco is SEEN-koh. Spanish vowels are short and clear, and they always sound the same. Uno is for counting; before a boy word it becomes un (un perro, one dog), and before a girl word it becomes una (una casa, one house).

lessons.title: Eleven to twenty
lessons.goal: Count from 11 to 20.

dialogue.en: One, two, three... ten! Very good, Sofía!

tip.title: Sixteen to nineteen
tip.text: Once to quince have their own names. From 16 to 19, Spanish says ten and six, ten and seven, squeezed into one word: dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve. Dieciséis has an accent on the last é. Once sounds like OHN-seh, not like the English word once.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Nice to meet you"?

lessons.title: Bright colors
lessons.goal: Name the bright colors and ask what color something is.

dialogue.es: Mamá, ¿de qué color es el cielo?
dialogue.en: Mom, what color is the sky?

dialogue.es: ¡Muy bien, Mateo! ¿Y el carro de la señora Díaz? ¡Es rojo!
dialogue.en: Very good, Mateo! And Mrs. Díaz's car? It's red!

tip.title: Es azul: no word for it
tip.text: ¿De qué color es? is word for word of what color is it? Answer with es and the color: es verde, it's green. Spanish doesn't need a word for it; es alone means it is. Many people say naranja for orange as well as anaranjado.

lessons.title: Black, white and in between
lessons.goal: Name black, white, gray and brown, and say light and dark.

dialogue.es: Sofía, ¿de qué color es tu perro?
dialogue.en: Sofía, what color is your dog?

dialogue.es: Es gris. ¿Y el carro de tu papá?
dialogue.en: It's gray. And your dad's car?

dialogue.es: Es azul claro. ¡Y el carro de mi mamá es verde oscuro!
dialogue.en: It's light blue. And my mom's car is dark green!

tip.title: Light and dark
tip.text: Add claro for light and oscuro for dark, after the color: azul claro, verde oscuro. In Mexico, brown is usually café, like the color of coffee; other countries say marrón. Spanish usually says blanco y negro, white first, where English says black and white.

lessons.title: The red car
lessons.goal: Put a color after a thing and make it match.
new: Mi color favorito es el verde.

dialogue.es: Sofía, ¿cuál es la casa de Ana?
dialogue.en: Sofía, which one is Ana's house?

dialogue.es: Es el carro de la señora Díaz.
Mi color favorito es el amarillo. ¿Y tú?
dialogue.en: My favorite color is yellow. And you?

dialogue.es: Mi color favorito es el verde.

tip.title: Colors match the thing
tip.text: The color usually comes after the thing: el carro rojo, the red car. Colors ending in -o change to -a for a girl word (la casa blanca) and add -s for more than one (las flores amarillas). Verde, azul and gris stay the same for boy and girl words. When you name a color on its own, it is a boy word with el: el verde.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "the white house"?

exercises.en: Say: My favorite color is green.
exercises.es: Mi color favorito es el verde.
Mi color favorito es el rojo. ¿Y tú?
exercises.answer: Mi color favorito es el azul.

lessons.title: My family
lessons.goal: Name your parents, brothers and sisters.

dialogue.es: Es mi papá. Se llama Miguel.
dialogue.en: That's my dad. His name is Miguel.

dialogue.es: Mi familia es mi mamá, mi papá, mi hermana y mi hermano.
dialogue.en: My family is my mom, my dad, my sister and my brother.

tip.title: Mamá or madre?
tip.text: Mamá and papá are what you call your parents, like Mom and Dad. Madre and padre are more formal, like mother and father. The accents on mamá and papá put the stress at the end: ma-MÁ, pa-PÁ. Careful: papa without an accent means potato in Latin America!

lessons.title: Grandparents, aunts and uncles
lessons.goal: Name grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins, sons and daughters.

dialogue.en: Mateo! Sofía! It's Grandma and Grandpa!

dialogue.es: ¡Hola, Mateo! Mira: tu tío Luis, tu tía Marta y tu primo Diego.
dialogue.en: Hi, Mateo! Look: your uncle Luis, your aunt Marta and your cousin Diego.
Laura, my girl, how are you?

dialogue.es: Muy bien. ¿Y tú, Luis? ¿Qué tal, hijo?
dialogue.en: Very well. And you, Luis? How's it going, son?

tip.title: Abuelo, abuela, abuelos
tip.text: Many family words change -o to -a for a girl or woman: hijo, hija; abuelo, abuela; tío, tía; primo, prima. For a group of boys and girls together, use the boy word with los: los abuelos is grandpa and grandma together. Parents often call their child hijo or hija as a loving nickname, and you will hear the short forms mijo and mija (from mi hijo, mi hija).

lessons.title: Older and younger
lessons.goal: Say how many brothers and sisters you have, who is older, and I love you.

dialogue.en: Sofía, do you have brothers or sisters?

dialogue.es: Sí. Tengo un hermano, Mateo. Mi hermano es menor.
dialogue.en: Yes. I have one brother, Mateo. My brother is younger.

dialogue.es: Yo tengo dos hermanos: una hermana y el bebé.
dialogue.en: I have two siblings: a sister and the baby.

dialogue.es: Sí, mi hermana es mayor. El bebé se llama Pablo.
dialogue.en: Yes, my sister is older. The baby's name is Pablo.

dialogue.es: Buenas noches, Sofía. Buenas noches, Mateo.
dialogue.en: Good night, Sofía. Good night, Mateo.
Good night. I love you, Mom.

tip.title: Te quiero
tip.text: Te quiero is the everyday way families and friends say I love you. Te amo also means I love you; it is stronger and is used mostly between partners and in songs, though some families use it too. With brothers and sisters, mayor means older and menor means younger.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I have two siblings"?

lessons.title: How do you feel?
lessons.goal: Ask how someone feels and say happy, glad, sad, tired or okay.

dialogue.en: I'm happy. I have a new friend!
That's great! And you, Sofía? Are you okay?

dialogue.es: Estoy cansada y un poco triste. Mi amiga Ana está en Sonora.
dialogue.en: I'm tired and a little sad. My friend Ana is in Sonora.

tip.title: Estoy and a feeling
tip.text: Use estoy (I am) for how you feel right now: estoy feliz, estoy cansado. Feelings that end in -o change to -a for a girl or woman, so Sofía says estoy cansada and Mateo says estoy cansado. Feliz and triste are the same for everyone.

exercises.en: I'm very tired. (a boy says it)

lessons.title: Ready, nervous, excited
lessons.goal: Say angry, bored, nervous, excited and ready, and tell someone not to worry.

dialogue.es: Sí, mamá. Estoy emocionada, pero un poco nerviosa.
dialogue.en: Yes, Mom. I'm excited, but a little nervous.
Mom, what about me? I'm ready.

tip.title: Listo: ready or clever
tip.text: With estoy, listo means ready: estoy listo. With es, it means clever: Mateo es listo, Mateo is smart. A girl or woman says lista, nerviosa, emocionada, enojada and aburrida.

lessons.title: Hungry, thirsty, sleepy
lessons.goal: Say you are hungry, thirsty, sleepy, cold, hot or scared.

dialogue.es: No te preocupes, Mateo. Es solo la lluvia.
dialogue.en: Don't worry, Mateo. It's just the rain.
Good night, son. I love you.

tip.title: Tengo hambre: I have hunger
tip.text: For hunger, thirst, sleepiness, cold, heat and fear, Spanish says tengo, I have: tengo hambre is word for word I have hunger. These don't change for boys and girls. Say tengo calor when you feel hot; estoy caliente means something different, so don't use it to say you feel hot.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Are you okay?"

lessons.title: Twenty-one to fifty
lessons.goal: Count past twenty and say 30, 40 and 50.

tip.title: Twenty-something
tip.text: From 21 to 29, the numbers are one word: veinte y uno became veintiuno. Watch the accents on veintidós, veintitrés and veintiséis. From 31 on, they are three words: treinta y cinco is thirty and five. Before a boy word, veintiuno becomes veintiún: veintiún años.

lessons.title: Sixty to one hundred
lessons.goal: Count by tens up to 100.

dialogue.en: Sofía, how do you say "sixty" in Spanish?
Very good! Eighty, ninety... and "one hundred"?

tip.title: Sesenta or setenta?
tip.text: The tens follow the small numbers: seis gives sesenta, siete gives setenta, ocho gives ochenta, nueve gives noventa. Sesenta has an s like seis, and setenta has a t like siete. Exactly 100 is cien; from 101 on it is ciento: ciento uno, ciento veinte.

exercises.en: Count by tens: sixty, seventy, eighty.

lessons.title: How old are you?
lessons.goal: Ask someone's age and say yours.
new: Mi papá tiene cuarenta y dos años.

dialogue.en: Hi! My name is Lucía. How old are you?

dialogue.es: Tengo siete años. Mi hermana tiene doce años.
Mi hermana Sofía tiene diez años.
¡Y mi papá tiene cuarenta y dos años!

tip.title: Having years
tip.text: Spanish says how many years you have: tengo ocho años is word for word I have eight years. Never use soy for your age. With an adult you don't know well, ask ¿Cuántos años tiene usted?, though many grown-ups would rather not be asked. Always write años with the ñ: without it, the word means something else.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask a friend "How old are you?"

exercises.es: Mi papá tiene cuarenta y dos años.
Mi papá tiene cuarenta y dos años.

exercises.en: Ask an adult politely: How old are you?

lessons.title: Days of the week
lessons.goal: Name the days of the week and say what day it is.

dialogue.en: That's great! And Grandma and Grandpa?

dialogue.es: Sábado y domingo con los abuelos.
dialogue.en: Saturday and Sunday with Grandma and Grandpa.

tip.title: Days with small letters
tip.text: Days of the week are not capitalized in Spanish: lunes, martes. To say on Monday, use el: el lunes. For every Monday, use los: los lunes. Lunes to viernes end in -s and look the same for one day or many.

lessons.title: Birthdays from January to June
lessons.goal: Name the first six months and say when your birthday is.
new: Mi cumpleaños es el diez de marzo.

dialogue.es: Mi cumpleaños es el diez de marzo. ¿Y tú?
dialogue.en: My birthday is March 10th. And you?

tip.title: Dates: the day comes first
tip.text: Spanish says the day, then de, then the month: el diez de marzo is March 10th. Use the plain number, not tenth. Months are not capitalized: enero, febrero, marzo.

exercises.es: Mi cumpleaños es el diez ___ marzo.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Today is Friday"?

lessons.title: July to December
lessons.goal: Name the last six months and say the first of the month.

dialogue.es: En diciembre. ¡Y tu primo Diego, en agosto!
dialogue.en: In December. And your cousin Diego, in August!
July, August, October, December... That's great!

tip.title: The first of the month
tip.text: For the first day of a month, people usually say el primero: el primero de enero. For every other day, use the plain number: el dos de enero, el quince de agosto. In a month, without a day, is en: en diciembre.

lessons.title: Today, tomorrow, yesterday
lessons.goal: Talk about today, tomorrow, yesterday, now, later and parts of the day.

dialogue.en: Dad, what about Grandma and Grandpa? Today?

dialogue.es: No, por la tarde. ¡Y todo el fin de semana!
dialogue.en: No, in the afternoon. And the whole weekend!

tip.title: Mañana has two meanings
tip.text: La mañana, with la, is the morning. Mañana on its own means tomorrow. Tomorrow morning is mañana por la mañana. In Mexico you will also hear en la mañana for in the morning.

lessons.title: What time is it?
lessons.goal: Ask the time and tell the time on the hour, half past and quarter past.

dialogue.es: No te preocupes. La fiesta de Ana es a las cuatro.
dialogue.en: Don't worry. Ana's party is at four.

tip.title: Es la una, son las dos
tip.text: For one o'clock, say es la una. For every other hour, say son las: son las dos, son las tres. Add y media for half past, y cuarto for a quarter past, and y with the minutes: son las seis y diez. In Mexico, a quarter to is cuarto para: son cuarto para las doce.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "It's one o'clock"?

exercises.en: Say: It's a quarter past four.

lessons.title: Morning, noon and night
lessons.goal: Say morning or night with the time, ask at what time, and say early or late.
new: Son las ocho de la mañana.
Son las nueve de la noche.

dialogue.es: Son las nueve de la noche. Es tarde.
dialogue.en: It's nine at night. It's late.

dialogue.es: A las ocho de la mañana.

tip.title: In the morning, at night
tip.text: In conversation, Spanish doesn't usually say a.m. and p.m. Add de la mañana (in the morning), de la tarde (in the afternoon or early evening) or de la noche (at night): son las ocho de la mañana. Noon is mediodía. ¿A qué hora? asks when something happens; answer with a las and the hour: a las siete.

exercises.es: Son las nueve de la noche.
Son las nueve de la noche.

exercises.en: Say: It's eight in the morning.
exercises.es: Son las ocho de la mañana.

lessons.title: Breakfast
lessons.goal: Name breakfast foods and drinks.

dialogue.es: Sí, huevos y pan. ¿Leche o jugo?
dialogue.en: Yes, eggs and bread. Milk or juice?

dialogue.es: Leche, por favor. Y un plátano.
Y yo, una manzana y agua.
dialogue.en: And for me, an apple and water.

tip.title: El agua
tip.text: Agua is a girl word, but you say el agua, because la agua would run two a sounds together and the first a of agua is stressed. Words that describe it still use the girl form: el agua fría, the cold water. With more than one, it goes back to las: las aguas.

lessons.title: Lunch and dinner
lessons.goal: Name lunch and dinner foods.

dialogue.en: Yes, Mateo! Chicken, rice, beans... and vegetables!

tip.title: Lunch, comida and cena
tip.text: In Mexico, the big meal of the day is in the early afternoon and is often called la comida. El almuerzo can mean lunch, or a late breakfast, depending on the family. La cena is the evening meal, usually lighter. Beans and tortillas are on many Mexican tables every day.

lessons.title: At the table
lessons.goal: Ask what there is to eat, ask for things politely and enjoy the meal.

dialogue.es: Mamá, tengo hambre. ¿Qué hay de comer?
dialogue.en: Mom, I'm hungry. What is there to eat?
Dad, can you pass me the salt?

dialogue.es: Tengo sed. Quiero agua, por favor.
dialogue.en: I'm thirsty. I want water, please.

tip.title: Asking nicely at the table
tip.text: People say ¡buen provecho! to anyone who is eating, even strangers at a restaurant. ¿Me pasas la sal? is word for word do you pass me the salt?, a friendly way to ask. Quiero (I want) is fine at home with por favor; at a restaurant many people say quisiera, I would like. Rico about food means tasty, not rich.

exercises.en: Can you pass me the salt?
Can you pass me the salt?

pairs: Can you pass me the salt?

exercises.en: Say: Can you pass me the salt?

lessons.title: Rooms of the house
lessons.goal: Name the rooms of a house and say you are at home.

dialogue.en: Welcome, Ana! This is my house.

dialogue.es: Esta es la sala y esta es la cocina.
dialogue.en: This is the living room, and this is the kitchen.

dialogue.es: El baño es azul. Ven acá, Ana. ¡Este es mi cuarto!
dialogue.en: The bathroom is blue. Come here, Ana. This is my room!

dialogue.es: Mamá, estoy en casa de Sofía.

tip.title: En casa
tip.text: Estoy en casa means I'm at home, with no la. At someone else's house, add de: estoy en casa de Sofía. In Mexico a bedroom is often called la recámara, but el cuarto works everywhere. Ven acá (come here) is said to one person you call tú.

exercises.answer: Can you pass me the salt?

lessons.title: Things in the house
lessons.goal: Name furniture and things around the house.

dialogue.es: ¡Mateo! Canela está en la cocina, en la silla.
dialogue.en: Mateo! Canela is in the kitchen, on the chair.
And not on the table, Canela!

tip.title: El sofá, la mesa
tip.text: Most words that end in -a are girl words: la mesa, la silla, la ventana. A few are boy words, like el sofá and el día, so learn each word with its el or la. La tele is short for la televisión, like TV in English.

exercises.en: Say: the door and the window

lessons.title: House rules
lessons.goal: Understand everyday requests at home, from washing hands to bedtime.

dialogue.es: Mateo, la cena. Lávate las manos.
Sofía, cierra la puerta, por favor.

dialogue.en: Yes, now. Turn on the light.

dialogue.es: Son las nueve. Es hora de dormir.

dialogue.en: Good night, Mom. I love you.

dialogue.es: Te quiero, Mateo. Apaga la luz.
dialogue.en: I love you, Mateo. Turn off the light.

tip.title: Telling one person what to do
tip.text: To tell a family member or friend to do something, use the tú command: limpia, cierra, prende, apaga. Lávate means wash yourself, with te stuck on the end, so lávate las manos is wash your hands. Spanish says las manos, the hands, because it is already clear whose.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Turn off the light"?

exercises.es: Mateo, limpia tu cuarto, por favor.

lessons.title: In the backpack
lessons.goal: Name school things and greet the teacher.

dialogue.en: And your backpack? The book? The notebook?

dialogue.es: Sí. Y el lápiz y la pluma.
dialogue.en: Yes. And the pencil and the pen.
Good morning! Welcome to the classroom.

tip.title: Maestra
tip.text: Students in Mexico often call their teacher maestra or maestro, just like that, instead of using the teacher's name. A man who teaches is el maestro. La pluma is the usual word for pen in Mexico; other countries say el bolígrafo. More than one pencil is los lápices.

exercises.en: The book is in the backpack.
exercises.es: El libro está en la mochila.

lessons.title: In class
lessons.goal: Follow what the teacher says and ask questions in class.

dialogue.es: Buenos días. Abran sus libros, por favor.
dialogue.en: Good morning. Open your books, please.

dialogue.es: Ese, a, hache, u, a, erre, i, te, a.
dialogue.en: S, A, H, U, A, R, I, T, A.
Teacher, may I go to the bathroom?

dialogue.es: Sí, Daniel. Y Lucas, siéntate, por favor.
dialogue.en: Yes, Daniel. And Lucas, sit down, please.

tip.title: One student or the whole class
tip.text: Levanta and siéntate are commands for one student. To the whole class, a teacher says abran (open, all of you) and siéntense (sit down, all of you). In Latin America, ustedes is the you for a group, friends or not, so sus libros here means your books. Al is a + el squeezed together: al baño, to the bathroom.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I have a question"?

wrong: How do you say it in Spanish?

exercises.en: May I go to the bathroom?
May I go to the bathroom?
Say: May I go to the bathroom?

lessons.title: Recess and good work
lessons.goal: Say you don't know, say you're done, and praise good work.

dialogue.en: Mateo, how do you say "recess" in Spanish?

dialogue.es: ¡Muy bien, Daniel! Escucha, Mateo: el recreo.
dialogue.en: Very good, Daniel! Listen, Mateo: el recreo.

tip.title: Sé and se
tip.text: No sé means I don't know. Sé with an accent is I know; se without an accent is a different little word, as in ¿cómo se escribe? Ya terminé means I'm done; word for word it is already I finished.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I don't know"?
